passage:
Monday: In the review, Jahnavi spoke fast. "What made you choose that? What was going through your head? Who approved it?" Sachin's chest went tight. He said, "It was in the brief," and stopped talking.
Tuesday: Sachin replied to every message with one word. He rehearsed his defence in the shower.
Wednesday: Jahnavi caught him at the coffee machine. "Yesterday my questions must have sounded like an attack. I'm sorry. Could you walk me through how the decision was made? I'd like to understand." Sachin looked up. "Sure. It began when the client changed the deadline, and I only had a day." Jahnavi nodded. "That helps. Thank you."

qa.q: What did Sachin say in the review after the fast questions?
qa.a: "It was in the brief."

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling during the barrage of questions?
qa.a: Attacked and defensive. His chest went tight, and he stopped talking, then replied with one word for the day.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi change on Wednesday?
qa.a: Jahnavi apologised for how the questions sounded and asked Sachin to walk through how the decision was made, with genuine curiosity.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have seen the first round of questions?
qa.a: As a way to understand a problem, without noticing how they sounded, until Jahnavi saw Sachin go quiet and reply with single words.

grounding: A person fired quick questions like why did you do that feels attacked; the same content asked with softer tone and curiosity gets better answers.

passage: Parul, I'm Binita, and I'll tell you about my first job at the newspaper. My editor, Mr Iqbal, would read my copy and bark, "Why did you write this? What were you thinking? Who told you that was a fact?" Every question felt like a slap. I stopped explaining. I just said, "Sorry," and my face went hot. Then I moved to another desk, under a woman called Sunita. Same mistake, same copy. She put it down and said, "Help me see how you got to this line?" I told her about my source, and even found the gap myself. The questions were nearly the same. The difference was in the voice. It stayed with me.

qa.q: What did Mr Iqbal bark at Binita's copy?
qa.a: "Why did you write this? What were you thinking? Who told you that was a fact?"

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when the editor asked the fast questions?
qa.a: Attacked and ashamed. Every question felt like a slap, so the face went hot and Binita only said sorry.

qa.q: What did Sunita do differently that helped Binita?
qa.a: Sunita put the copy down and asked calmly, "Help me see how you got to this line?", which invited an explanation.

qa.q: How might Sunita have seen Binita's mistake?
qa.a: As something to understand, since she asked how Binita got there, and was interested in the source and the reasoning.

grounding: A person fired quick questions feels attacked; the same content in a softer voice brings better answers.

passage: The storm had shut the highway, the warehouse was flooded to the ankles, and the shipment to Delhi was a day late. Binita had made a call at 6 am: hold the trucks until the road reopened. At nine, her manager Indu arrived, wet and tense. "Why did you hold the trucks? What were you thinking? Who told you to decide that? Do you know what the client will say?" Binita felt her chest tighten. Every question sounded like an accusation. She mumbled, "I thought it was safer," and stopped talking. Indu went to her office. An hour later she came back with two cups of tea. "Sorry, Binita. I was panicking. Can you walk me through how you decided?" Binita breathed out. She explained the road closure, the driver's call, the flooded bridge. Indu listened. "That was the right call," she said.

qa.q: What time did Binita decide to hold the trucks?
qa.a: At 6 am.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when Indu fired questions at her?
qa.a: She felt attacked and tense, her chest tightening, so she mumbled one line and stopped talking.

qa.q: What changed when Indu came back with tea?
qa.a: Indu apologised and asked the same thing with a softer tone and real curiosity, so Binita could explain clearly.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when she first arrived?
qa.a: Indu was panicking and tense, worried about the client and the delay.

grounding: Shows a person hit with rapid, accusing questions feeling attacked, and the same questions asked softly getting a better answer.

passage: Rehana got home to the Andheri flat at 1 am, after a colleague's farewell. Her flatmate Irawati was waiting on the sofa. "Where were you? Why didn't you answer? What were you thinking? Do you know what time it is?" Rehana felt like she was in a police station. She snapped, "I'm not a child," and went to her room. Neither slept well. The next morning Irawati made tea and sat on the edge of Rehana's bed. "I'm sorry about last night. I was so worried I came out swinging. Can you tell me what happened?" Rehana softened. "My phone died at the party. I should have borrowed someone's to text you. I'm sorry you were scared." Irawati nodded. "Can we agree to text if we'll be after midnight?" "Yes. Deal."

qa.q: What time did Rehana get home?
qa.a: At 1 am.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when Irawati fired questions at her?
qa.a: She felt attacked and treated like a child, as if she were in a police station, so she snapped and left.

qa.q: What did Irawati do the next morning that worked better?
qa.a: She apologised and asked 'Can you tell me what happened?' in a calm, curious way, which helped Rehana explain and apologise too.

qa.q: How was Irawati feeling the night before?
qa.a: She was worried and scared, which made her questions come out harsh.

grounding: Shows a person hit with rapid, accusing questions feeling attacked, and the same content asked gently getting a better answer.

passage:
"You quit? Why would you quit? What were you thinking? What about the loan? Did you even talk to anyone?"
"Tarun, stop. You sound like a lawyer."
"I'm just asking!"
"You're firing at me. I can't think." Ayesha turned toward the window.
Tarun stopped. Breathed. Sat down beside her. "Sorry. I got scared. Can I try again?"
"...Okay."
"What happened at work that made you want to leave?"
Ayesha was quiet. Then: "My manager's been shouting at me for months. On Friday he threw a file at the wall near my head. I couldn't go back."
Tarun's face changed. "Oh, Ayesha. I didn't know."
"You didn't ask like that before."
"I'm asking now. What do you need?"
"Just help me tell Ammi. And maybe look at job listings with me."

qa.q: What did Ayesha's manager throw at the wall?
qa.a: A file, near Ayesha's head.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when Tarun fired his first questions?
qa.a: Ayesha felt attacked and overwhelmed, unable to think, and turned away toward the window.

qa.q: What did Tarun change that led to a better answer?
qa.a: Tarun apologised, slowed down and asked one open, caring question: what happened at work that led to leaving.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel once he heard the real reason?
qa.a: Tarun felt shocked and sorry, realising how little was known about what Ayesha had been going through.

grounding: Shows a person fired with quick, accusing questions feeling attacked, and the same content asked softly bringing out the real story.

passage: I'm Vinita, and last month I sent a bank-holiday notice to the wrong mailing list. Nirmala called me into the glass cabin before I had even sat down. "Why would you send it? What was going on in your head? Who approved it? Did you even check?" Each question landed before I had finished answering the last. My mind went blank. I kept saying "I don't know", which was not even true. I just felt cornered. Two days later Nirmala came to my desk with two cups of tea. "I came at you too fast on Monday," she said. "Can you walk me through what the send looked like from your side?" Almost the same questions, really. But this time I remembered the filter that had reset overnight, the rushed deadline, the second check nobody did. We fixed the filter together in twenty minutes. Looking back, I had the answers all along. I just couldn't reach them while I was busy defending myself.

qa.q: What had reset overnight?
qa.a: The filter had reset overnight.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling during the quick questions in the glass cabin?
qa.a: Vinita felt attacked and cornered; the mind went blank and "I don't know" came out even though it was not true.

qa.q: What could Nirmala try the next time a mistake happens on the team?
qa.a: Ask one calm question at a time, like "walk me through it from your side", and wait for the whole answer before asking the next.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see the Monday meeting two days later?
qa.a: Nirmala seems to see that the rapid-fire questions got only "I don't know", and that a gentler tone was what finally brought out the real causes.

grounding: Shows a person who goes blank under quick, attacking questions and then gives full answers when the same questions come with a softer tone and real curiosity.
